# Ensure you’re insured: Scooter-rental insurance and city requirements

One of the most frequently overlooked aspects of [starting a scooter rental business](https://joyride.city/blog/money-you-can-earn-with-a-scooter-sharing-business/) is the need for insurance. Here are the common requirements of U.S. cities and the type/amount of insurance required to operate your fleet.

### Where to look

Since scooter-share fleets are such a new business venture, the available insurance carriers willing to underwrite a policy for these types of businesses have typically been limited. But things have changed over the past year as more businesses grow and the market continues to expand.

In order to access the appropriate carriers, you will need to speak to an insurance broker that specializes in ride-share insurance or startup insurance (a broker is the individual who will connect you with the insurance carrier as most carriers will not deal with you directly). While you may successfully find brokers through an internet search, Joyride has partnered with [three global insurance providers](https://joyride.city/blog/looking-for-micromobility-insurance-weve-got-you-covered/) to offer our customers exclusive preferred rates and access to informational resources like workshops and webinars. As a one-stop hub for getting your shared mobility business seamlessly off the ground, it only makes sense for us to connect our operators with the right insurance provider, too.

### What type of insurance do you need?

Most municipalities will require you to have what is known as Commercial General Liability insurance (CGL) in order to operate within their borders. CGL is the insurance that will cover the costs in the event one of your riders gets hurt or damages someone’s property while using your scooters. You’ll typically be required to have at least US$1 million to US$2 million in coverage, but possibly up to US$10 million depending on the location. These figures are the maximum amount that will be paid out in any one claim.

In addition to a CGL policy, you may want to investigate obtaining what is known as 1st party coverage. While not required, this is the insurance that will cover the costs of your scooters if they are ever damaged or stolen. Note: wear-and-tear is excluded under these policies — don’t expect the insurance company to pay for your overused scooters!

### How much coverage is needed

Premiums are not typically calculated by fleet size, so don’t let a desire to launch a big fleet deter you from getting insurance information! Instead, most premiums are calculated by the amount of revenue generated by the business. Large, litigious cities (typically coastal ones) will usually have higher premiums, while cities in the mid-U.S. states can expect some reductions.

Policies can be split to help cover additional types of claims while reducing your premiums. For example, you can purchase $1 million to $2 million in CGL and have an additional $5 million in what is known as Excess Liability insurance or Umbrella Coverage. These policies will only be triggered in the event your CGL policies limits are exceeded. As this insurance is supplementary, your premiums will likely be somewhat cheaper.

Not many people like talking about insurance, but it’s important to come to your city prepared. Walking through the door with your policy in place will go a long way to getting your fleet launched.

### Conclusion

You’ll need at least $2 million in coverage under what is known as a Commercial General Liability Insurance policy. Premiums are calculated based on the revenue generated by a fleet. As for best practices, we recommend approaching your city with your policy already in place. [Contact us](https://joyride.city/get-started/) today to learn more about how we can make that happen.

# Everything you need to know about micromobility fleet insurance

September 14, 2023

min. read

For shared mobility operators, fleet insurance should be one of the top priorities. No matter the size or composition of your fleet, having the right insurance can offer peace of mind by protecting your business from unforeseen situations

However, the insurance question can sometimes seem daunting – especially if you're [new](https://www.atommobility.com/blog/how-much-capital-do-you-need-to-start-your-own-shared-mobility-business) to the industry. In this article, we will explore the key things you need to know about insuring your shared micromobility fleet.

## Why you need insurance

Operating a shared mobility fleet isn’t always smooth sailing. Accidents can happen – whether it's a minor fender-bender or something more severe. Insurance serves as your safety net, offering financial coverage for repairs, replacements, and even potential legal obligations after an incident.

Here are the main reasons why insurance should be one of the top priorities for shared mobility fleet operators:

‍**Legal compliance**: In many places, insurance for shared mobility fleets is a legal requirement. You probably want to comply with these regulations to avoid any potential fines, penalties – or even the suspension of your operations.

**Financial security**: Insurance also helps keep your business going financially, no matter what happens. Without insurance, accidents, vehicle damage, or theft can seriously impact your finances. Comprehensive insurance coverage can ensure that you're not left scrambling to cover any unexpected expenses.

## Understanding shared micromobility insurance

When it comes to insuring micromobility fleets, part of the challenge stems from the fact that the market is relatively new. Some insurance underwriters avoid dealing directly with micromobility because it's seen as an unfamiliar market.

This is where brokers like [Cachet](https://cachet.me/en/e-scooter-insurance-fleet-management/) and others specializing in micromobility insurance come in. They partner with various insurance underwriters to provide coverage for operators in this field.

When it comes to shared micromobility, insurance coverage generally has a twofold role: safeguarding assets and handling third-party engagement in the event of accidents.

**Liability coverage:** Securing third-party public liability insurance for shared mobility fleets is not just a matter of choice – in some places, it's mandated by law. This insurance serves to protect pedestrians and riders in the unfortunate event of accidents, providing financial coverage for injuries and damages that may arise. In other words, it's a safety net that offers peace of mind to operators.

When it comes to mandatory third-party liability insurance, the negotiations with the insurance company usually begin by figuring out what the local authorities require to give them a permit. After that, the insurance policy is adjusted to meet the specific demands outlined by these authorities.

**Physical damage coverage:** This covers the repair or replacement costs of vehicles if they are damaged due to accidents, collisions, vandalism, or theft. Depending on the policy, physical damage coverage may also extend to equipment like GPS devices, charging stations, and other hardware.

‍

## What decides your insurance premium payments?

The amount you'll pay in premiums depends on various factors that are specific to your business This includes your fleet's makeup, where and how you operate, and the level of coverage you're aiming for.

**Fleet usage**: The more a shared micromobility fleet is used, the more chances there are for things to go wrong. When a fleet is in high demand and used often, there's a greater likelihood that something might happen that requires insurance coverage.

**Rider behavior:** Insurance companies also consider the fleet's ability to predict and manage undesirable rider behavior. Reckless riding, improper parking, or violating traffic rules can significantly increase the risk of accidents and incidents. Operators that have better measures in place to anticipate and mitigate such behaviors can demonstrate a lower risk profile to insurance providers.

**Value of the fleet**: How much your vehicles are worth individually and as a fleet will affect how much you pay for insurance. If your vehicles are expensive, your insurance premiums will be higher because it would cost more to replace them if they get damaged or lost.

**Size of the fleet:** Operators can often negotiate more favorable insurance rates for proportionally larger fleets. As the number of vehicles increases, the overall expected risk is distributed and “diluted” as a result – which translates to lower premiums per vehicle.

However, some brokers like Cachet have embraced a broader approach, ensuring that smaller and medium-sized fleets can also benefit from insurance coverage.

**Technology implementation:** Shared mobility services that employ technologies like GPS tracking, telematics, and IoT devices can provide insurers with valuable data. This data can then help assess driver behavior and usage patterns, enabling insurers to offer more accurate and tailored premium rates. This also takes into account how simple it is for scooters to be stolen and how well the recovery processes function – which can also play a role in insurance expenses.

**Where you operate**: The location in which your fleet operates is another important factor. From the insurer’s perspective, different areas pose varied levels of risk. For example, urban mobility – which is associated with a higher risk of accidents – may incur higher premiums compared to vehicles used in rural areas.

**Level of coverage**: The level of coverage you choose directly affects how much you pay in premiums. Opting for higher coverage limits means you get more comprehensive protection, but obviously, it also means your insurance costs go up.

## Choosing the ideal insurance for your fleet

Every shared mobility fleet and business is different, so your insurance needs will depend on things like the type and size of your fleet, where you operate, how much risk you're comfortable with, and of course – how much you are willing to pay.

For example, do you require coverage for specific risks, like vandalism, or perhaps your fleet is composed of premium vehicles that are more expensive? To make it more relatable, let's dive into a practical case of a shared micromobility operator's experience with insurance.

### How Hoog found the right insurance with Cachet

The concept behind [Hoog Mobility](https://hoogmobility.ee/) is to revolutionize transportation in smaller Estonian towns. They recognized the need for efficient and eco-friendly local travel and brought a shared mobility solution often seen in big cities but missing in smaller communities: electric scooters.

Cash-strapped mobility startups often worry about potential damage or vandalism happening to their shared vehicles. This concern is shared by traditional insurance companies too. As a result, these insurers might hesitate to provide coverage for shared scooters, and if they do – it's usually at a higher cost.

Faced with this challenge, Hoog initially operated without insurance due to the steep expenses. But that changed when Cachet provided them with a customized insurance solution that perfectly suited the company's needs. Hoog also realized that the initial worry about vandalism wasn't as much of an issue as they thought. But still – having insurance for their fleet turned out to be a sound financial decision that gave them peace of mind.

## Concluding remarks

Don't underestimate insurance – it's just as crucial as having a top-notch fleet and solid [scooter sharing software](https://www.atommobility.com/use-cases/scooter-sharing-software). Insurance is best approached proactively – discovering you've cut corners after an unforeseen event will cost you significantly more.

Getting insurance for shared micromobility might be a bit trickier since it's still a new concept, but we've seen that even smaller fleets can make it work – it's just a matter of finding a suitable partner who understands your needs.

At the end of the day, insurance isn't merely about meeting legal requirements – it showcases your dedication to safety, responsible operations, and the well-being of everyone involved in your mobility business.

Who will operate Europe’s robotaxi fleets?

🤖 Who will actually operate Europe’s robotaxi fleets? Autonomous driving may remove the driver, but it doesn’t remove the work behind the car. Robotaxis still need charging, cleaning, maintenance, depots, customer support and someone managing the fleet every day. Early projects in Zagreb, Madrid and London illustrate different stages of deployment and how AV technology providers, fleet operators and booking platforms can work together. Taxi, rental and car-sharing companies already handle many of these tasks. What would it take to turn that experience into an autonomous fleet business?

October 21, 2026

min. read

Read post](/blog/who-will-operate-europes-robotaxi-fleets)

For a taxi fleet owner, autonomous vehicles may seem to remove the most important part of the current business – the driver. But even without drivers, someone still needs to take care of the cars. They need to be owned or financed, charged, cleaned, inspected and repaired. Someone also needs to manage depots, deal with incidents, help customers and make sure enough cars are available.

The first robotaxi services and tests in Europe are already showing how this could work. The company that develops the autonomous driving technology does not always own or operate the cars. The app where customers book their rides may come from another company too. This could leave an important role for taxi, rental, car-sharing and other fleet companies that already know how to manage vehicles.

## **What changes when the driver disappears?**

A taxi company today manages both cars and drivers. Drivers need to be recruited, scheduled, paid and supported. With a driverless fleet, these tasks would eventually disappear, but most of the work related to the cars would stay.

Autonomous cars still need charging or refuelling, cleaning, tyres, inspections, repairs and insurance. They also need somewhere to park when they are not working. If there is an accident or a technical problem, someone needs to deal with it and get the car back on the road. Customer support is still needed too when there are problems with bookings or payments, or when someone leaves something in the car.

Some of these tasks may even become more important. Robotaxis are expensive, and every hour a car spends charging, being cleaned or waiting for maintenance is an hour when it cannot take passengers. [Moove](https://www.moove.io/autonomous-vehicles), for example, already provides fleet ownership, depots, charging, maintenance and 24/7 operations for autonomous vehicles.

Drivers also do more than drive: they notice damage, report faults, help passengers and respond when something goes wrong. Without a driver, these responsibilities need clear processes and dedicated support. Existing fleet experience is an advantage, but operators will need to adapt it to vehicles running without someone behind the wheel.

## **Who actually runs a robotaxi service?**

There can be several companies behind one robotaxi ride. One provides autonomous driving technology, another may own the cars, and a local company can take care of the fleet. A platform such as Uber can then connect the cars with passengers. Sometimes one company may do several of these things, but this is not always the case.

Zagreb is one example. [Pony.ai](http://pony.ai) provides the autonomous driving system, [Verne](https://www.verne.co/) owns and operates the fleet, and [Uber](https://www.uber.com/lt/en/) connects it with customers through its app. Autonomous rides became commercially available through Uber in August 2026 with a licensed operator onboard. On 10 September, Pony.ai and Verne also started fully driverless passenger test rides on a 22-kilometre route connecting parts of Zagreb with the airport. These are still limited test rides, not a fully driverless service across the whole city.

A similar model is being tested in Madrid. [WeRide](https://www.weride.ai/), Uber and [AVOMO](https://avomo.com/) received permission in September 2026 to start testing and mapping under Spain’s ES-AV framework. The first 20 vehicles have an onboard specialist. WeRide provides the autonomous technology, Uber connects the cars with passengers, and AVOMO takes care of fleet operations. Commercial operations are planned for later in 2026, but the current permit is for testing and preparation rather than a general driverless taxi service.

In London, [Wayve](https://wayve.ai/) and Uber launched supervised autonomous passenger rides in September 2026. Customers can be matched with an autonomous vehicle through the Uber app, but there is still a licensed driver in the car.

## **Europe is preparing for larger robotaxi fleets**

The plans for the next few years are already much bigger. Pony.ai and Uber announced in August 2026 that they plan to deploy more than 2,000 robotaxis in Europe, starting with Zagreb and later expanding to four more European cities.

[Bolt](https://bolt.eu/en-lv/) and [Lucid](https://lucidmotors.com/) announced another partnership in September, with Bolt aiming to deploy at least 25,000 autonomous Lucid vehicles across European cities. This is a future target, not 25,000 cars already operating today.

How these fleets are owned and operated may also be different from one city to another. Local regulations, available vehicles, charging and depot infrastructure and partnerships will all have an effect on how each service is set up.

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/643e15786c3c1ff52f75bd0d/6ad8aaa70a5d735867405147_245f252b.jpeg)

Who will operate Europe’s robotaxi fleets?

## **What could this mean for taxi companies?**

Taxi companies already do many of the things that would still be needed with an autonomous fleet. They maintain cars, deal with insurance and incidents, provide customer support and make sure enough vehicles are available. Some also already have their own depots, charging infrastructure or maintenance partners.

One possible model can already be seen in Zagreb. A local company owns and operates the autonomous fleet, while a larger ride-hailing platform brings customers. In the future, an existing taxi company could potentially have a similar role. Instead of managing cars and drivers, it could manage autonomous cars that receive bookings through a larger platform.

This does not mean platforms such as Uber will always rely on other companies to own the cars. Uber’s 2026 agreement with Rivian includes up to $1.25 billion in milestone-dependent investment and says that Uber or its fleet partners may purchase the autonomous vehicles. Uber is also developing infrastructure for autonomous fleets. Different ownership models are therefore possible.

## **What about rental and car-sharing companies?**

Autonomous vehicles could also become interesting for rental and car-sharing companies, although this is probably further in the future. These businesses already manage vehicles, maintenance, cleaning, charging, bookings, customer accounts and payments, so much of the practical work is similar.

Autonomous driving could also change how rental and sharing cars are moved. Today, an employee may need to drive a car from one location to another. In the future, the vehicle could potentially do this itself within an area where autonomous driving is approved. It could even become possible for a rental car to drive itself to a customer’s pickup point.

## **How do you measure a robotaxi fleet?**

Without drivers, it becomes especially important to understand how much time each vehicle is actually working. Every hour spent charging, being cleaned, waiting for maintenance or simply sitting unused means less time carrying paying passengers.

Some useful KPIs could be available hours per vehicle, paid trips per vehicle each day, revenue per available vehicle/day, empty kilometres, charging and maintenance downtime, cost per trip and incidents that need human help. These are most popular robotaxi industry KPIs of what a company could measure during a pilot.

For example, if cars spend too much time waiting to charge, the charging setup may need to change. A lot of empty kilometres could mean the cars are not in the right places, while too much maintenance downtime could make a vehicle more expensive to operate.

## **How could local companies enter the market?**

For either model, the business case depends on the partnership terms: who finances the vehicles, who carries the risk when demand is low, and how revenue and operating costs are shared. Operators should assess what remains after vehicle financing, insurance, charging, maintenance and partner fees. Depots, local service teams and reliable fleet availability could make an operator a valuable partner, but profitability still needs to be demonstrated.

One option for taxi fleets would be to work with an autonomous driving company and a larger ride-hailing platform. The local company could own or manage the cars and take care of the fleet, while customers book their rides through the larger platform.

Another option could be possible in cities where large ride-hailing platforms are not present or have limited coverage. A local company could work with an approved AV provider while using its own app, bookings, payments, customer support and fleet management.

In both cases, a company cannot simply buy autonomous cars and start offering rides. The technology needs to be approved, and local rules have to allow the service. These rules will also be different across Europe. Great Britain, for example, introduced its Automated Passenger Services permitting framework in 2026. Services similar to taxis or private hire vehicles need consent from the relevant local authority, while responsibility for the autonomous driving technology and the passenger service are treated separately.

## **What can fleet companies do now?**

A company does not need to have autonomous cars today to start preparing. A good first step is understanding the current fleet in detail – what each vehicle costs, how many hours it is available, how much time it spends charging or being repaired, and when cars are used the most.

Charging, cleaning, maintenance and depot processes are also worth looking at because all of these will still be needed with autonomous vehicles. A company interested in an AV pilot can then choose a location and use case, look at the local permit process and start talking to autonomous driving technology providers.

The software will also need some preparation. Customers still need to book and pay for rides, while the company needs fleet information, customer support, reporting and connections between its own systems and the AV technology. Starting with a small pilot makes it possible to test all of this before trying to build a larger service.

## **Where could ATOM Mobility fit?**

ATOM Mobility already provides many of the software functions used by taxi, ride-hailing, rental and sharing companies, including customer apps, bookings, payments, fleet management, maintenance tasks, analytics and APIs. Its [ride-hailing software](https://www.atommobility.com/products/ride-hailing) includes passenger and driver apps, dispatch, payments, fleet data, analytics and integrations. The [ATOM Mobility API](https://www.atommobility.com/api) can also exchange data about vehicles, bookings, rides, payments, telemetry and maintenance tasks.

ATOM Mobility does not provide autonomous driving technology. This would come from a specialised AV company, and each project would have its own technical requirements and local approvals. For an AV pilot, ATOM Mobility could work with the fleet company and AV provider on the rider experience, integrations, fleet management and the data needed to measure how the pilot is working.

Navigating the shift: Key takeaways from ATOM Connect Rental 2026 in Riga

ATOM Connect Rental 2026 brought rental operators, aggregators, and technology partners together in Riga on October 8 to discuss the future of vehicle rental. Key topics included margin pressures, customer friction, data-driven fleet decisions, insurance, and keyless operations. The central takeaway: growth depends on improving customer experience and fleet efficiency, with practical steps operators can take today.

October 12, 2026

min. read

Read post](/blog/navigating-the-shift-key-takeaways-from-atom-connect-rental-2026-in-riga)

On October 8, 2026, we gathered on the panoramic top floor of the AC Hotel by Marriott in Riga for **ATOM Connect Rental 2026**.

Following the community-first approach of our past mobility summits, our goal for this edition was simple: avoid the noise, generic pitches, and sales booths of conventional trade shows. Instead, we brought together an intimate room of car rental operators, regional franchise managers, aggregators, and technology pioneers to have an open, unfiltered conversation about where vehicle rental is heading and what it actually takes to get there.

The day’s agenda reflected that intent. Rather than treating digitization as a buzzword, the sessions explored the operational realities of the industry: from global macroeconomic forces to the high-stakes friction points at the physical rental desk.

Here is a recap of the key discussions, industry data, and takeaways from the summit.

## **The macro view: Three forces redefining vehicle rental** [(Frost & Sullivan)](https://www.frost.com/)

Opening the morning keynotes, **Frost & Sullivan** set the strategic foundation by examining how vehicle rental is shifting from an asset-heavy model to a digitally enabled, flexible mobility ecosystem.

Their analysis highlighted **three forces** currently reshaping the industry:

1. **Disruptive Technologies:** App-based journeys, automated digital identity verification (AI KYC), and keyless access are quickly becoming baseline customer expectations.
2. **Internal Cost & Margin Pressures:** Repair costs, vehicle turnaround times, insurance inflation, and fragmented software are squeezing fleet utilization. Connected operations are now critical to protecting margins.
3. **Transformative Megatrends:** Electrification, changing travel patterns, and sustainability regulations are forcing operators to rethink fleet acquisition and pricing strategies.

The main takeaway from their presentation was clear:

*"The winners will not simply manage more vehicles - they will manage the customer, fleet, and ecosystem more intelligently."*

Looking ahead, Frost & Sullivan stressed that future value will come from **experience-led rental models** (low-touch, personalized journeys), **commercial and LCV subscriptions**, and **ecosystem partnerships** that maximize revenue per vehicle, customer, and trip.

## **A front-row reality check: Why car rental is the toughest service in travel** [(EconomyBookings)](https://www.economybookings.com/)

Following lunch, **Vitalijs Cvetkovs**, Head of Commerce at **EconomyBookings.com**, delivered a refreshingly candid, data-backed session on why car rental remains the most friction-heavy customer journey in travel.

While booking a flight or hotel is relatively straightforward, car rental forces the customer to decode dozens of brands, ACRISS vehicle codes ("or similar"), deposit rules, insurance tiers, and fuel policies. Drawing on data from over a million annual bookings, Vitalijs pinpointed the **four friction points** where the industry loses customers:

* **Choice Overload:** Searches returning 700+ vehicle variations across 70+ brands overwhelm customers. Aggregators must prioritize smart, predictive ranking to surface the 10 most relevant cars rather than an endless list.
* **The Broken Pricing Reflex:** Unlike flights and hotels, car rental prices often drop in the final weeks before pickup. This trains travelers to book speculatively, monitor prices, cancel, and rebook - driving up cancellation rates across the board.
* **The Credit Card Wall:** EconomyBookings' audit revealed that **less than 30% of European counter offers accept debit cards**. With modern travelers increasingly relying on neobanks, turning customers away at the desk because they lack a credit card for the deposit creates major operational friction. Low-deposit and debit-friendly models are the inevitable direction of travel.
* **The Counter as the "Emotional Summit":** The counter is where booking expectations collide with operational realities. Their review data confirms an uncomfortable pattern: *the lower the daily rental rate, the rougher the expected pickup experience*.

Vitalijs concluded with a crucial commercial insight: In the era of AI and instant review summaries, poor customer experiences are instantly visible. **Customer experience is the only sustainable retention driver**, and aggregators and operators must work together to absorb friction rather than pass it on to the traveler.

## **Ground-level Intelligence: Spatial AI and next-gen insurance**

Beyond macro trends and customer journeys, the technical sessions focused on practical tools operators can deploy today:

* [Anadue](https://anadue.com/) **(Urban Mobility at the Speed of Thought):** Mike Manchip showcased their **SuperFlexMap** platform, demonstrating how spatial data drives branch profitability. By combining census statistics, commuting patterns, hotel density, and car ownership data, operators can perform gap analysis to identify affluent, car-free neighborhoods that lack rental desks - replacing intuition with empirical site selection.
* [Datafolio](https://www.datafolio.com/) **(Unlocking Value in Add-On Insurance):** Datafolio addressed the headache of unpredictable fleet coverage, showing how AI risk modeling (UBRA) and transparent, app-based micro-insurance can turn fleet insurance from an operational cost burden into an EBITDA generator.

## **Operationalizing the future: The** [INVERS](https://invers.com/en/) **fireside chat**

Closing out the afternoon, ATOM Mobility hosted a fireside session with **INVERS** to discuss the nuts and bolts of deploying "digital rental-ready" fleets.

The session focused on practical execution. Using real-world examples, the discussion highlighted how telematics, CAN-bus hardware, and remote immobilizers enable traditional operators to launch **virtual stations**, service off-airport locations, and automate replacement vehicle workflows without increasing staff overhead.

The key takeaway: modernizing a fleet does not require an immediate, risky transition away from the counter. Hybrid operations allow established rental businesses to introduce 24/7 keyless handovers alongside their standard operations.

**The Value of the Closed Room**

As presentations concluded and conversations moved into the evening networking mixer overlooking Riga, the feedback mirrored what made previous ATOM Connect events special: the value is entirely in the room.     
  
By capping attendance and curating an audience of active industry operators, conversations went deeper than high-level presentations.  A sincere thank you to all our speakers, partners, and guests who joined us in Riga. The vehicle rental sector is evolving quickly, and we are proud to provide the space where the industry comes together to map out what comes next.     
  
Stay tuned for our next ATOM Connect events by following us on [LinkedIn!](https://www.linkedin.com/company/35636919/)

# Scooter Theft Insurance: How to Protect Your Scooter and Your Wallet

Scooters are a fun, affordable, and eco-friendly way to get around, but their compact size also makes them a prime target for theft.

Whether you ride a classic Vespa or an electric scooter, protecting your ride goes beyond just locking it up. In this guide, we’ll break down what scooter theft insurance is, how to prevent scooter theft, and how GEICO can help you ride with confidence.

## Does Scooter Insurance Cover Theft?

[Scooter insurance](/scooter-insurance/) can cover theft if you have the right coverage. Standard liability insurance covers damage you cause to others, not your own scooter. To be protected against theft, you’ll need comprehensive coverage, which helps pay for your scooter if it’s stolen or damaged by something other than a collision, like vandalism or weather.

Keep in mind, insurance requirements may vary by scooter type and state laws. Smaller mopeds and e-scooters might not need coverage to operate legally, while scooters with engines of 50cc and up often do. Either way, if theft protection is what you’re after, comprehensive insurance is the way to go. For a deeper understanding of how moped and scooter insurance differ, you can check out [Moped vs Scooter page](/scooter-insurance/moped-vs-scooter-insurance/).

## Why Are Scooters Targeted for Theft?

Scooters are a convenient form of transportation, but that convenience makes them a popular target for thieves. They're lightweight and portable, which means someone can quickly lift one into a vehicle and drive off. They’re often parked outside in public spaces without much protection, making them easier to grab when no one’s looking.

Plus, many scooters lack advanced anti-theft features, like alarms or immobilizers, which gives thieves even more opportunity. That’s why having the right insurance—and a few smart security habits—can make a big difference in keeping your ride safe.

## 7 Insurance Specialist Tips to Prevent Scooter Theft

Whether you’re commuting to work or parking downtown for a coffee run, a few smart habits and tools can go a long way in keeping your scooter safe. Here are seven ways to help protect your ride:

### 1. Mix Up Your Parking Routine

Thieves often look for patterns. If you park in the same spot at the same time every day, it’s easier for someone to plan a theft. Try to vary your routes and parking times when commuting or running errands to keep would-be thieves guessing.

### 2. Choose Safe Parking Locations

Whenever possible, park in well-lit, high-visibility areas. If you can, park in a secure garage or a monitored lot. These locations may have parking fees, but they can be worth the extra protection.

### 3. Use Multiple Locking Mechanisms

Layer your defenses. Use a combination of heavy-duty chain locks and D-locks to secure both the wheels and frame to a fixed object. Steering locks alone usually aren’t enough, so don’t rely on them as your only form of protection.

### 4. Install Audible Alarms and GPS Trackers

Loud alarms can scare off thieves. Add a GPS tracker for another layer of security—some even connect to your smartphone to alert you if your scooter moves unexpectedly, making recovery more likely if it’s stolen.

### 5. Add a Kill Switch or Immobilizer

A hidden kill switch cuts power to the ignition, making it impossible to start the scooter until it’s disabled. It’s a simple but effective theft deterrent. You can install it yourself, or hire a professional for added security.

### 6. Personalize Your Scooter

A one-of-a-kind scooter is much harder to resell. Consider a custom paint job, decals, or even VIN engraving on major parts. These not only make your scooter easier to identify but can also discourage thieves from trying to strip it for parts.

### 7. Cover It

Out of sight, out of mind. A basic scooter cover might not seem like much, but it can make your ride less noticeable—and less tempting—to thieves passing by. It also adds a layer of effort that some thieves simply don’t want to deal with.

## How to Properly Lock a Scooter

Locking your scooter might seem straightforward, but a few simple techniques can make a big difference in deterring theft. Follow these best practices to help keep your scooter safe and sound:

* Lock Both Wheels: If your scooter has a front and rear wheel lock point, secure both. Thieves may remove a single locked wheel to get away with the rest of the scooter.
* Secure to an Immovable Object: Always anchor your scooter to something sturdy like a bike rack, metal post, or ground anchor. A locked scooter that isn’t attached to anything can still be lifted into a vehicle.
* Keep Chains Elevated: Avoid letting your chain or lock rest on the ground. When it’s elevated, it’s much harder for thieves to use bolt cutters or leverage tools to break it.
* Point Keyholes Downward: Position lock keyholes facing the ground. This small trick makes lock-picking more difficult and time-consuming, which is something most thieves want to avoid.

## What to Do If Your Scooter Is Stolen

If your scooter goes missing, acting fast is key. To increase the chance of recovery and get the claims process started:

1. File a Police Report Immediately: Report the theft to local law enforcement as soon as possible. The sooner you file, the better the odds of recovering your scooter, especially if you have a GPS tracker or custom features that help identify it.
2. Gather Documentation: To file a claim, you’ll need a few pertinent details ready, including your scooter’s VIN, purchase receipts, recent photos, and a copy of the police report. The more info you can provide, the smoother the claims process will be.
3. [Contact GEICO](/contact-us/): If you have comprehensive coverage, give us a call or [start your claim online](/claims/). We’ll walk you through the process and help you take the next steps.

## How Much Does Scooter Theft Insurance Cost?

The cost of scooter theft insurance depends on several factors, including where you live, the local theft rates, your scooter’s type and value, and any built-in security features like alarms or GPS trackers. Your personal claims history also plays a role in determining your premium.

The good news? GEICO offers competitive rates and [discounts](/save/discounts/) to help you get the protection you need without breaking the bank.

## GEICO's Coverage Options for Scooter Riders

GEICO offers a range of coverage options designed specifically for scooter riders, so you can enjoy every drive.

* [**Liability Coverage**](/information/aboutinsurance/auto/liability-insurance/): Helps cover property damages or injuries you cause to others while riding.
* [**Collision Coverage**](/information/aboutinsurance/auto/collision-coverage/)[:](https://www.geico.com/information/aboutinsurance/auto/collision-coverage/) Helps pay for damage to your scooter if you're in an accident, regardless of fault.
* [**Comprehensive Coverage**](/information/aboutinsurance/auto/comp-coverage/)[:](https://living.geico.com/saving/insurance-101/comprehensive/) Covers non-collision incidents like theft, vandalism, or weather damage.
* **Emergency Roadside Service & Trip Interruption**: Get help with towing, flat tires, or lodging if your trip is disrupted by a covered incident.
* **Accessory Coverage**: Protects aftermarket upgrades like custom seats, paint, or tech accessories. It may also pay for damaged protective gear like helmets.

## Ready to Protect Your Scooter?

Scooter theft can happen in a matter of seconds, but with the right insurance, you won’t be left footing the bill. From comprehensive coverage to protection for your gear and custom parts, GEICO has flexible options to help keep you and your ride covered.

**Ready to protect your scooter?** Get a free [scooter insurance quote](/scooter-insurance/) from GEICO today and hit the road knowing you’re backed by coverage you can count on.

## FAQs About Scooter Theft Insurance

* Is scooter theft covered by basic insurance?

  Basic liability insurance only covers property damage or injury you cause to others. To be protected against scooter theft, you need comprehensive insurance.
* What kind of scooter insurance do I need to be protected from theft?

  To safeguard your scooter against theft, vandalism, and other non-collision events, you’ll want comprehensive coverage. This is an optional add-on, meaning you’ll have to select it when purchasing scooter insurance.
* Does GEICO offer insurance for electric scooters?

  Yes, GEICO offers coverage for many types of scooters, including electric models. Coverage options and requirements can vary based on the type, speed, and usage, so it’s best to get a quote tailored to your ride.
* Can I insure accessories like a helmet or custom parts?

  Yes, GEICO offers optional coverage for safety riding apparel like helmets and jackets, and custom parts and equipment coverage for things like aftermarket upgrades and tech add-ons. These are not standard coverages, so make sure you add them to your policy when getting a quote.
* What should I do if I forgot to lock my scooter and it was stolen?

  Start by filing a police report right away, then contact GEICO to file a claim if you have comprehensive coverage. Forgetting to lock your scooter doesn’t automatically disqualify you, but every claim is reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

# Bike Rental Insurance: What You Actually Need

LendControl Team··7 min read

One bad crash. That is the distance between a profitable bike rental business and a lawsuit that wipes you out.

* **Bike rental insurance is not optional** — but most new operators either buy too much of the wrong coverage or not enough of the right kind.
* **The result is wasted money** — or worse, a gap that leaves you exposed when a rider gets hurt or a bike gets stolen.
* **This guide breaks down exactly which policies you need** — what they cost, and how to structure your coverage so you are protected without overpaying.

![Bike rental shop owner reviewing insurance documents at front desk](/wp-content/themes/lendcontrol/assets/images/blog/bike-rental-shop-owner-reviewing-insurance-documents.jpg)

A bike rental shop owner reviewing insurance paperwork at the front desk

## Why one rider injury can end your bike rental business

Bicycle accident settlements vary widely — from five figures to over **$1 million** in severe cases involving head trauma or permanent disability.

* **A tourist rents your bike, hits a pothole, breaks a collarbone** — their attorney comes after your business
* **Without liability coverage** — you are paying that settlement out of pocket
* **A single six-figure claim** — means closing the doors for most small operators

This is not a hypothetical risk. Bikes go out every day to riders with varying skill levels, on roads and trails you do not control. The question is not whether an incident will happen — it is whether you will be covered when it does.

## The four types of bike rental insurance you need

Not every policy is equally important. Here are the four that matter for a bicycle rental insurance setup, ranked by priority.

### General liability insurance

This is the non-negotiable one. General liability covers bodily injury to riders and third parties, plus property damage claims. If a customer crashes into a parked car on your rental bike, this policy handles the claim.

Most commercial landlords require **$1 million per occurrence** in general liability coverage before they will even sign a lease with you. Event venues and tourism boards often require the same minimum plus a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as an additional insured.

### Commercial property insurance

If you lease or own a physical shop, commercial property insurance covers the building contents — your repair tools, front desk equipment, signage, and fixtures — against fire, theft, vandalism, and weather damage. It does not cover the bikes themselves when they are out on rental (that requires a separate policy).

### Inland marine / equipment floater

This is the one most new operators miss. A standard commercial property policy only covers your bikes while they are inside your shop. Once a bike leaves the premises — which is the entire business model — you need an equipment floater (technically called inland marine insurance) to cover theft, accidental damage, and loss while the bike is with a customer or in transit.

### Workers’ compensation

Required in most states the moment you hire your first employee. Workers’ comp covers medical costs and a portion of lost wages when an employee is injured on the job. For bike rental staff doing physical work — loading bikes, doing repairs, riding to delivery locations — the risk is real.

![Bike rental operator tagging fleet bike with asset number in workshop](/wp-content/themes/lendcontrol/assets/images/blog/bike-rental-operator-tagging-fleet-bike-workshop.jpg)

A bike rental operator attaching an asset tag to a rental bike in the workshop

## What each policy costs for a small bike fleet

Here is what a typical 15-to-25-bike rental operation can expect to pay annually. These are real ranges from insurance providers and industry sources.

| Coverage Type | Annual Cost | What It Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General liability ($1M per occurrence) | [$540](https://www.insureon.com/small-business-insurance/general-liability/cost)–[$810/year](https://www.thehartford.com/general-liability-insurance/cost) | Bodily injury, property damage to third parties |
| Inland marine / equipment floater | [~$350/year](https://www.insureon.com/small-business-insurance/inland-marine) | Bikes while rented out, in transit, or stored off-site |
| Workers’ compensation | [~$643/year](https://www.insureon.com/small-business-insurance/workers-compensation/cost) | Employee injuries on the job |
| **Business Owner’s Policy (BOP)** | **[$648–$996/year](https://www.insureon.com/small-business-insurance/business-owners-policy/cost)** | **Bundles liability + property + business interruption** |

**If you buy each policy separately**, expect to pay **$1,800 to $3,100 per year** total. A BOP bundles general liability, commercial property, and business interruption into a single policy — usually at a lower combined cost than buying them individually.

For a small fleet operation, a BOP plus an equipment floater plus workers’ comp (if you have staff) covers the critical bases:

* **20-bike fleet without employees:** roughly $1,200 to $2,000 per year
* **20-bike fleet with a small team:** roughly $1,500 to $2,700 per year

**Ready to track every bike in your fleet and protect your rental records?** [Join the waitlist](/waitlist/) — no credit card required.

## E-bikes change the insurance math

If your fleet includes e-bikes — and in 2026, it probably should — your bike rental liability insurance picture gets more complicated.

E-bikes are heavier, faster, and more expensive than pedal bikes. A standard rental e-bike costs **$1,200 to $2,500** compared to **$300–$800** for a city cruiser. That higher asset value means higher equipment floater premiums.

But the bigger issue is liability. E-bikes reach speeds of 20–28 mph depending on class, which increases the severity of potential injuries. Some insurers classify e-bikes differently than pedal bikes, and a few standard bicycle rental insurance policies exclude motorized vehicles entirely.

Before you add e-bikes to your fleet, confirm three things with your insurer:

* **Your general liability policy explicitly covers e-bike rentals.** Do not assume it does.
* **Your equipment floater covers the full replacement value** of each e-bike, not just the depreciated value.
* **Your policy covers all three e-bike classes** (Class 1, 2, and 3) if you plan to stock multiple types.

Specialized insurance providers offer policies built specifically for bike and e-bike rental operations. If your current insurer treats e-bikes as an afterthought, it is worth getting a quote from a specialist.

## Waivers and contracts: your first line of defense

Insurance pays claims after something goes wrong. Waivers and rental contracts reduce your legal exposure before anything happens.

Every rider should sign a liability waiver and rental agreement before touching a bike. A solid rental contract covers:

* **Assumption of risk** — the rider acknowledges cycling carries inherent risk
* **Liability release** — limits your responsibility for injuries during normal use
* **Damage responsibility** — defines who pays for damage, theft, or loss
* **Return conditions** — specifies return time, condition expectations, and late fees
* **Security deposit terms** — documents the deposit amount ($50–$200 per bike is standard) and refund conditions

Paper waivers work, but they create a storage nightmare and are easy to lose. Digital waivers signed at booking time are faster, more organized, and hold up better in court because they capture timestamps and electronic signatures.

With rental management software, digital contracts can be built into the booking flow. Customers sign before pickup, and every signed agreement is stored automatically — no filing cabinets, no missing paperwork. You can set up rental contracts that capture the waiver, deposit authorization, and rental terms in one step.

![Customer signing digital bike rental waiver on tablet at outdoor rental stand](/wp-content/themes/lendcontrol/assets/images/blog/customer-signing-digital-bike-rental-waiver-tablet.jpg)

A customer signing a digital waiver on a tablet at an outdoor bike rental stand

## How to keep your premiums low

Bike rental insurance does not have to eat your margins. Here are practical ways to reduce what you pay:

* **Bundle with a BOP.** A Business Owner’s Policy costs less than buying general liability and commercial property separately. Ask your agent about adding an equipment floater to the same policy.
* **Require signed waivers from every rider.** Insurers view documented risk acknowledgment favorably. Consistent waiver compliance can improve your renewal rates.
* **Charge damage waiver fees to customers.** A $5–$15/day optional damage waiver fee offsets your deductible costs and creates a revenue stream.
* **Collect security deposits.** A $50–$200 refundable deposit per bike discourages reckless riding and covers minor damage without filing a claim. Every claim you avoid keeps your premiums stable.
* **Maintain your fleet.** Documented maintenance logs show insurers you are reducing risk. Bikes with working brakes, proper tire pressure, and functional lights are less likely to cause incidents.
* **Increase your deductible.** If you can absorb a $1,000 or $2,500 deductible instead of $500, your annual premium drops. Only do this if your cash reserves can handle it.
* **Shop multiple providers.** Get quotes from at least three insurers, including both generalist providers and specialists who focus on rental operations.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does bike rental insurance cost per year?

A small bike rental operation with a 15-to-25-bike fleet typically pays **$1,200 to $3,100 per year** for full coverage, depending on whether you bundle policies and whether you have employees. General liability alone runs **[$540](https://www.insureon.com/small-business-insurance/general-liability/cost)–[$810/year](https://www.thehartford.com/general-liability-insurance/cost)** for $1 million in coverage. A Business Owner’s Policy ([$648–$996/year](https://www.insureon.com/small-business-insurance/business-owners-policy/cost)) can reduce total costs by bundling liability and property coverage.

### Do I need separate insurance for e-bikes?

Not always a separate policy, but you need to confirm your existing coverage explicitly includes e-bikes. Some general liability and equipment policies exclude motorized vehicles. E-bikes are heavier, faster, and more expensive to replace — all factors that can affect your premiums and coverage limits. Ask your insurer directly and get the answer in writing.

### Is bike rental insurance required by law?

There is no federal requirement, but many states require workers’ comp if you have employees. Beyond legal mandates, commercial landlords almost universally require **$1 million in general liability** before signing a lease. Tourism boards and event venues also require proof of insurance. In practice, you cannot operate a legitimate bike rental business without it.

### Can a signed waiver replace insurance?

No. A waiver reduces your legal exposure by documenting that the rider accepted the risk, but it does not eliminate liability. Courts can and do override waivers, especially in cases involving negligence (like renting out a bike with faulty brakes). Waivers and insurance work together — the waiver is your first defense, and insurance is your financial backstop.

### What happens if a customer steals a rental bike?

If you have an inland marine or equipment floater policy, the theft is covered up to your policy limit minus the deductible. Without that coverage, the loss is entirely yours. This is why security deposits ($50–$200) and documented rental agreements matter — they create a paper trail and a financial deterrent. For high-value e-bikes, GPS tracking adds another layer of protection.

## Protect your bike rental business before your first booking

Getting your bike rental insurance right is not exciting, but it is the difference between a business that survives its first incident and one that does not. Start with general liability and an equipment floater at minimum. Add a BOP if you have a physical shop. Layer in workers’ comp when you hire.

Pair your insurance with signed waivers, security deposits, and solid rental contracts to build a defense that covers you from every angle. And use rental management software to keep your contracts, booking records, and fleet documentation organized — because when a claim happens, the operator with clean records is the one who comes out whole.
